rows.answer: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique and approach that enables large language models (LLMs) to integrate with document retrieval systems and incorporate new information from external data sources [3][5]. Instead of relying solely on static training data, RAG allows LLMs to first refer to a specified set of documents or pull relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources before responding to user queries [3]. This process supplements the model's pre-existing training data, helping the LLM stick to facts, reduce AI hallucinations, and utilize updated or domain-specific information without requiring a full model retraining [3].

The data that RAG references is typically converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in the form of a large vector space [2]. This process can be used on unstructured, semi-structured, or structured data, such as knowledge graphs [2]. Additionally, chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so that the retriever can find details in it [1][3]. These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval [2].
Hybrid search combines traditional text search (also known as full text search) results with the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from a vector search [3].
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can be used on unstructured data (which is usually text), semi-structured data, and structured data such as knowledge graphs [3].

Project Treble is a major re-architecture of the Android OS framework introduced by Google in May 2017 with the announcement of Android 8.0 [1]. It is designed to make updating devices to newer Android versions easier, faster, and less costly for manufacturers [1]. 

Project Treble separates the vendor implementation—which is the device-specific, lower-level software written by silicon manufacturers—from the Android OS framework by using a new "vendor interface" [1]. Because no formal vendor interface existed in Android 7.0 and earlier, device makers had to update large portions of Android code to move a device to a newer operating system version [1]. With Project Treble, the stable vendor interface provides access to hardware-specific parts, allowing device makers to deliver new Android releases simply by updating the OS framework without any additional work from silicon manufacturers [1]. Additionally, Project Treble is described as a framework designed to streamline the development and deployment of Android updates via Google Play Services, reducing the involvement of manufacturers in the update process [3].
